title: A Glasshouse for the Inventory
premise: Oscar Villalobos, a court translator who has spent a decade softening testimony into almost-silence, hears an unrecorded song on late-night radio — one their late mother composed and never let anyone write down. The broadcast leads them back to the glasshouse nursery of their childhood neighborhood, now slated for demolition, where three estranged figures from an old photograph are keeping the song alive as evidence in an unofficial reckoning with the man who stole it. As the last bus route to the old district is rerouted, Oscar must choose between translating for the man who wronged them all or finally speaking in their own voice. In the end, the song is recorded once, badly, by everyone together, and the glasshouse falls — but the language survives in mouths that learned to say it whole.
about_author: Tamsin Okonkwo is the pen name of a former interpreter who grew up between two languages and one demolished neighborhood. Their fiction has appeared in small journals that pay in copies, and this is their second novel.

chapters.title: The Almost-Said
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A day in the courtroom shows how Oscar translates testimony into softer versions of itself, erasing their own mother tongue word by word. At night, they rehearse phrases they never send. Emotional beat: the ache of self-erasure disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: A Song With No Address
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Half-asleep on the night bus, Oscar hears a radio DJ play an untitled song credited to 'found tape.' It is their mother's lullaby, the one she sang once and forbade recording. Emotional beat: vertigo — grief arriving as recognition.

chapters.title: The Photograph on the Fridge
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Digging through a shoebox, Oscar finds the old photograph: four children outside the glasshouse nursery, faces half-turned away. One face is theirs; another belongs to a stranger they've spent ten years not forgiving. Emotional beat: dread dressed as curiosity.

chapters.title: Last Stop Before Rerouting
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Notices announce the 47 bus line will be rerouted in six weeks, severing the old neighborhood from the city grid. Oscar rides it to the end of the line without getting off. Emotional beat: a deadline made physical.

chapters.title: The Glasshouse Still Stands
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Behind chain-link, the derelict nursery greenhouse survives, ferns swallowing broken benches. Someone has hung wind chimes made of tuning forks. Emotional beat: the past refusing to be rubble.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Frame
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Inside, Oscar meets Marisol, the girl from the photograph, now middle-aged and running an unofficial archive of the neighborhood's confiscated recordings. She recognizes Oscar instantly and says nothing kind. Emotional beat: hostility with history underneath.

chapters.title: Evidence of Singing
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol explains the archive: tapes seized decades ago by Aurelio Sanch, a producer who recorded the neighborhood's musicians, kept the masters, and erased the makers' names. The lullaby is Exhibit One. Emotional beat: righteous anger learning patience.

chapters.title: What Mother Wouldn't Write Down
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Flashback chapter: young Oscar watching their mother sing the lullaby once, then burn the only written copy, saying some things must live in bodies or not at all. Emotional beat: tenderness curdling into a rule Oscar resents.

chapters.title: The Third Face
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The fourth person in the photograph was Teo, now a lawyer representing — of all people — Aurelio Sanch, who is dying and wants to 'return' the tapes on his own terms. Emotional beat: betrayal wearing a suit.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Teo meets Oscar in a diner and offers a deal: sign a release letting Sanch donate the archive to a university under his name, and everyone gets the music back legally. Oscar refuses. Emotional beat: the law offering everything except justice.

chapters.title: Listening Party for the Disappeared
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. In the glasshouse, neighbors gather weekly to play seized tapes aloud — names spoken before each track, restoring credit by mouth. Oscar attends and is asked to translate a Yoruba-inflected testimony no court ever wanted. Emotional beat: found family assembling itself around sound.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar begins losing words from their mother tongue mid-sentence, substituting English, and starts a private ledger of what remains. Marisol catches them writing and softens, barely. Emotional beat: fear that identity is a finite inventory.

chapters.title: Sanch, Dying, Talks
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar visits Sanch's hospital room as a translator-for-hire and finds him lucid, unrepentant, and full of justifications: he 'saved' the music from oblivion. He asks Oscar to interpret his apology for the record. Emotional beat: the trap of being the bridge.

chapters.title: The Translation Refusal
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Asked to render Sanch's apology into the neighborhood's language, Oscar discovers there is no honest translation — his words have no equivalent — and refuses on the record. Emotional beat: first act of open defiance; terror and relief.

chapters.title: What Marisol Buried
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol confesses she was the one who leaked the lullaby to the radio — bait to draw the photograph's children home — because she couldn't finish the reckoning alone. Emotional beat: guilt met with unexpected gratitude.

chapters.title: The Reroute Begins
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Crews tear up the 47's route; detour signs bloom like weeds. The glasshouse receives its demolition notice, effective in nine days. Teo warns that once the building goes, the archive loses its legal standing as an 'occupied premises.' Emotional beat: time compressing.

chapters.title: Sides of the Tape
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Torn between client loyalty and the photograph, Teo discovers Sanch's will leaves the masters to whoever can prove authorship — proof Sanch deliberately destroyed. Teo makes a copy of the destruction ledger. Emotional beat: conscience outbidding career.

chapters.title: The Hearing in the Greenhouse
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interwoven. The neighbors hold their own proceeding in the glasshouse: testimonies, tapes, names restored aloud, with Oscar translating everything into both languages, fully, for the first time. Sanch arrives in a wheelchair to hear it. Emotional beat: justice performed outside any courtroom.

chapters.title: Forgiving the Stranger
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Alone with Sanch afterward, Oscar realizes the stranger in the photograph they could never forgive was themselves — the child who stayed silent while the tapes were taken. They speak the forgiveness aloud, in the mother tongue, and mean it. Emotional beat: climax of the interior arc.

chapters.title: Nine Days
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. With Teo's ledger, the group files authorship claims; the university offer collapses; Sanch, changed or simply tired, signs the masters over to the named musicians. The last bus makes its final run down the old route, packed with neighbors singing. Emotional beat: victory arriving quietly, on schedule.

chapters.title: One Take, Badly Sung
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. On demolition morning, the community records the lullaby once — off-key, layered, imperfect — everyone's voices including Oscar's, unedited. The excavators wait until the take ends. Emotional beat: grief and joy in the same breath.

chapters.title: The Inventory Survives
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Epilogue a year later: the archive lives in a storefront near the new bus line; Oscar translates court testimony straight now, no softening, and teaches children the lullaby's verses. The ledger of borrowed words closes with a note: nothing left to lose. Emotional beat: wholeness — a language kept by giving it away.
